title: AP Precalculus

modules.title: Rational functions and missing inputs
modules.focus: Distinguish a hole from a vertical asymptote.
explanation: A rational function is defined only where its original denominator is nonzero. Factoring the numerator and denominator identifies shared factors. Cancelling a shared factor simplifies nearby values but leaves a hole at the excluded input.

A denominator zero that remains after simplification may produce a vertical asymptote. Compare leading powers for end behaviour. Keep the domain, intercepts and asymptotes together when judging whether a proposed graph matches a formula.

steps: Factor x²-4=(x-2)(x+2), so f(x)=x+2 for x≠2.
The graph is that line with a hole at (2,4), not a vertical asymptote.

misconception.claim: Every denominator zero is a vertical asymptote.
misconception.correction: A cancelled zero can instead create a removable hole.

questions.prompt: Where is the vertical asymptote of 3/(x+4)?
Find the average rate of change of x² over [1,4].
questions.hint: Divide output change by input change.
checkpoints: Keep the interval endpoints in order.

questions.prompt: Find the hole and vertical asymptote of (x²−1)/(x²+3x+2).
Find the average rate of change of f(x)=1/x on [1,4].
checkpoints: Output change is −3/4; input change is 3.
hints: Output change is −3/4; input change is 3.

notes.title: Reasoning through rational functions and missing inputs
paragraphs: A rational expression inherits every zero-denominator restriction before simplification. A common factor can remove the visible denominator while leaving a hole in the original graph. An uncancelled denominator zero may instead create a vertical asymptote, determined by nearby behaviour. Horizontal asymptotes describe distant inputs and need not prevent the graph from crossing that height at finite inputs. Average rate of change compares two outputs over an interval; it is not an instantaneous slope. Keep domain, intercepts and asymptotes separate so a simplified formula does not erase information about the original function.

steps: Factor numerator (x−3)(x+3) and denominator (x−3)(x+2).
For x≠3,−2 the reduced expression is (x+3)/(x+2).
At x=3 the reduced value is 6/5; at x=−2 its denominator remains zero.
workedExamples.conclusion: There is a hole at (3,6/5), vertical asymptote x=−2 and horizontal asymptote y=1.

flashcards.front: What creates a hole after cancellation?
flashcards.back: An input excluded by a cancelled denominator factor.

flashcards.front: What controls a horizontal asymptote for equal degrees?
Can a graph cross a horizontal asymptote?
What is average rate of change?

modules.title: Exponential growth and logarithmic inversion
modules.focus: Find an unknown time in a multiplicative model.
explanation: Equal input increments produce equal ratios in an exponential model. In A(t)=A₀b^t, A₀ is the value at t=0 and b is the factor for one input unit. A percentage increase p corresponds to b=1+p when p is a decimal.

A logarithm reverses exponentiation. Solving b^t=c gives t=ln(c)/ln(b) for b>0 and b≠1, with c>0. An exponential fit describes the observed range; extrapolation assumes its growth mechanism continues.

workedExample.prompt: A culture model is N(t)=200(1.5)^t. When does it reach 675?
steps: Divide by 200 to obtain 1.5^t=3.375.
Since 1.5³=3.375, t=3 time units.

misconception.claim: A 20% increase means adding 0.2 each period.
misconception.correction: It means multiplying the current amount by 1.2.

questions.hint: Apply the same logarithm to both sides.

questions.prompt: An amount decreases by 15% each year. Write its model from an initial 80.

questions.hint: Nine hours contains three half-life intervals.
questions.prompt: A model starts at 160 and halves every 3 hours. Find its amount after 9 hours.
checkpoints: Nine hours contains three half-life intervals.
hints: Nine hours contains three half-life intervals.

notes.title: Reasoning through exponential growth and logarithmic inversion
paragraphs: An exponential model applies a constant multiplicative factor over equal input intervals. A percentage decrease uses a factor between zero and one; subtracting the percentage repeatedly would instead give a linear model. Logarithms undo exponentiation and are useful when the desired input is not an obvious whole number. Take logarithms only of positive quantities in a real-valued calculation. The fitted growth factor is an assumption about the modelled interval, so extrapolation can fail when resources or conditions change. The coefficient represents the amount at input zero, not an additional recurring contribution.

workedExamples.prompt: A model is N(t)=500(0.8)^t. When does it fall to 200?
steps: Divide by 500 to obtain (0.8)^t=0.4.
Take logarithms: t ln(0.8)=ln(0.4).
Both logarithms are negative, so their ratio is positive.

flashcards.front: How do you solve aᵗ=b for a>0, a≠1 and b>0?
What distinguishes exponential from linear change?
flashcards.back: A constant ratio rather than a constant difference.

flashcards.front: What does N₀ represent in N=N₀aᵗ?

modules.title: Reading a periodic model
explanation: For y=D+A sin(Bt+C), |A| is the amplitude and D is the midline. The period is 2π/|B| when angles are in radians. A phase shift changes timing, whereas D shifts every output vertically.

A physical context limits the meaningful domain and may constrain the range. In polar coordinates, a point uses a radius and angle rather than two perpendicular coordinates; convert with x=r cos θ and y=r sin θ.

workedExample.prompt: A height model is h(t)=7+3 cos(πt/4). Find its range and period.
steps: Cosine ranges from -1 to 1, so height ranges from 4 to 10.
The angular coefficient is π/4, giving period 2π/(π/4)=8.

misconception.claim: The coefficient of t is the period.
misconception.correction: It determines how fast the angle changes; period is its reciprocal times 2π.

questions.prompt: Find the amplitude and midline of 5-2 sin(3t).

questions.hint: Use cosine for x and sine for y.

questions.prompt: Find the period and range of y=2+5 sin(4t).

questions.hint: Use x=r cos θ and y=r sin θ.
questions.prompt: Convert polar coordinates (6,5π/6) to Cartesian form.
checkpoints: Use x=r cos θ and y=r sin θ.
hints: Use x=r cos θ and y=r sin θ.

notes.title: Reasoning through reading a periodic model
paragraphs: A sinusoidal model separates vertical position, amplitude, angular frequency and phase. The amplitude is nonnegative even when the coefficient is negative; that sign changes the phase or reflection. The period is 2π divided by the magnitude of the angular coefficient when the angle is in radians. A phase shift must be found after factoring that coefficient from the input expression. Test a convenient time to distinguish a maximum, minimum or midline crossing. A periodic model repeats indefinitely mathematically, although a physical application may only justify it within a limited interval.

steps: The midline is 10 and amplitude is 4, giving range [6,14].
The angular coefficient π/3 gives period 6.
At t=2 the cosine is 1, so h=6, a minimum.
workedExamples.conclusion: The graph has period 6 and a minimum at t=2.

flashcards.front: Is a negative coefficient a negative amplitude?
How is period calculated in radians?

flashcards.back: The centre height of the oscillation.

flashcards.front: How can a phase interpretation be checked?
flashcards.back: Substitute a time producing a known sine or cosine value.

modules.title: Vectors and matrix transformations
modules.focus: Follow a point through a linear transformation. This unit is not assessed on the AP Exam.
explanation: A vector records a directed change. Add its components to combine displacements and use the square root of the sum of squared components for magnitude. Position and displacement are related but distinct quantities.

A two-by-two matrix transforms a column vector through row-by-column multiplication. The order of transformations matters because matrix multiplication is generally not commutative. This extension unit belongs to the course framework but is not assessed on the AP Precalculus Exam.

workedExample.prompt: Apply the matrix [[0,-1],[1,0]] to the column vector (3,2).
steps: The first component is 0(3)-1(2)=-2.
The second is 1(3)+0(2)=3, giving (-2,3), a quarter-turn anticlockwise.

misconception.claim: Applying two transformations in either order always gives the same point.
misconception.correction: Matrix products can differ when their order is reversed.

questions.prompt: Apply [[1,2],[0,1]] to (3,−1) and explain the unchanged component.
checkpoints: The second row [0,1] copies the original y-coordinate.

notes.title: Reasoning through vectors and matrix transformations
paragraphs: Vectors encode both magnitude and direction, so component operations preserve more information than adding magnitudes alone. A matrix transformation forms each output component from a row dot product with the input column. Applying two transformations means multiplying in their order of action: the rightmost matrix acts first. Reversing the order can change the result. A zero determinant means some nonzero direction collapses and the map cannot be inverted. These are selected topics from the course’s functions involving parameters, vectors and matrices unit; that unit is outside the AP Precalculus exam assessment scope.

workedExamples.prompt: Apply a horizontal stretch by 2, then a quarter-turn anticlockwise, to (1,3).
steps: The stretch gives (2,3).
The rotation sends (x,y) to (−y,x).
Apply it to (2,3) to obtain (−3,2).
workedExamples.conclusion: The combined transformation gives (−3,2). Reversing the order would give (−6,1).

flashcards.front: How is a matrix output component calculated?
flashcards.back: A matrix row is dotted with the input column.

flashcards.front: Which matrix acts first in ABv?
